monitored_text: Resources / Machining Design / Hydraulic System: Definition and Examples Hydraulic System: Definition and Examples Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 30 min read Published November 24, 2026 A hydraulic system is a mechanical system that transmits force and performs work through pressurized, incompressible fluid moving through a closed circuit of components. Hydraulic systems operate by converting mechanical input energy at a pump into fluid pressure energy, then reconverting that pressure at an actuator into linear or rotary mechanical output. The core components include a pump, reservoir, directional control valves, actuators (cylinders and motors), filters, and a heat exchanger, all connected by high-pressure lines rated from 7 MPa to 70 MPa depending on application. Hydraulic systems appear in excavators, injection molding machines, aircraft flight controls, metal-forming presses, brake assemblies, and material testing frames. The force output of a hydraulic actuator is the product of fluid pressure and piston area: a 150 mm bore cylinder at 35 MPa delivers over 619 kN of output force, a ratio unachievable with pneumatic or mechanical alternatives of equivalent size. Precise motion control, high force density, and overload protection through pressure relief valves make hydraulic power the preferred solution across industrial, mobile, and aerospace machinery. Xometry supplies precision-machined hydraulic components, including cylinders, manifold blocks, and valve bodies across the full range of system pressures and configurations. What Is a Hydraulic System? A hydraulic system is a mechanical power transmission system that uses a pressurized, incompressible liquid to generate, control, and transfer force to perform useful work. The system relies on controlled fluid movement through interconnected components, producing linear force from cylinders or rotary torque from motors, with outputs ranging from a few kilonewtons in precision equipment to over 100,000 kN in large industrial presses. Hydraulic systems are widely used in industrial and mobile machinery because fluid power transmits large forces through small-diameter lines with precise controllability. An excavator boom generates digging forces exceeding 150 kN from a hydraulic cylinder with a 150 mm bore diameter at a working pressure of 35 MPa, a force-to-size ratio unachievable with comparable mechanical linkages. Industrial machinery, including injection molding machines, metal-forming presses, and material testing frames, depends on hydraulic systems for high force density (power output per unit volume), smooth motion control, and the ability to hold loads statically without continuous energy input. Xometry provides precision-machined hydraulic components across a wide range of system pressures and configurations. How Is a Hydraulic System Defined in Engineering? A hydraulic system is defined in engineering as a power transmission system that converts mechanical input energy into fluid pressure energy at a pump, transmits that pressure energy through a fluid circuit, and reconverts it to mechanical output energy at an actuator to perform work. The definition encompasses the full energy conversion chain: a prime mover (electric motor or combustion engine) drives a hydraulic pump, which pressurizes fluid and delivers it at controlled flow rates through distribution lines to cylinders, motors, or other actuators that execute the required mechanical motion. Hydraulic systems are essential in heavy equipment because they transmit power efficiently over distance through flexible hoses, allow force multiplication through differential piston areas, and provide inherently overload-protected operation through pressure relief valves set at the maximum allowable working pressure. Operating pressures in industrial hydraulic systems range from 7 MPa in light-duty mobile equipment to 70 MPa in high-force hydraulic presses and forming machines. The ratio of output force to input force is determined by the ratio of actuator area to pump displacement, allowing engineers to design precise force and motion profiles for each application. Is a Hydraulic System Based on Pascal's Law? A hydraulic system is based on Pascal's Law, which states that pressure applied to an enclosed, incompressible fluid at rest transmits equally and undiminished in all directions throughout the fluid. French mathematician Blaise Pascal established the law in 1653, and it provides the theoretical basis for all hydraulic force multiplication and pressure transmission functions. The practical consequence of Pascal's Law in hydraulic system design is force multiplication: a pressure of 20 MPa applied through a pump acts equally on every square millimeter of fluid-contacted surface throughout the circuit, including the face of a large-bore actuator cylinder. A cylinder with a bore area of 5,000 mm² at 20 MPa generates an output force of 100 kN from an input force applied to a much smaller pump piston. The law further explains why pressure relief valves protect every component simultaneously: when the relief valve opens at maximum system pressure, that pressure limit applies circuit-wide, preventing localized overloading at any single actuator or fitting. How Does a Hydraulic System Work? A hydraulic system works by pressurizing incompressible fluid at a pump, directing it through control valves and distribution lines to actuators, where fluid pressure acts on piston or vane surfaces to generate mechanical force and motion. The pump draws fluid from a reservoir, raises its pressure from near-atmospheric to the system's working pressure (7 to 70 MPa), and delivers it at a controlled volumetric flow rate into the pressure circuit. Directional control valves route pressurized fluid to the correct actuator port, determining the direction of cylinder extension or motor rotation. Pressure control valves set the maximum operating pressure and manage load-holding behavior, while flow control valves regulate actuator speed by restricting fluid volume per unit time. Return fluid from the low-pressure side of the actuator flows back through the return line to the reservoir, where it is filtered, cooled, and recirculated. The closed-loop fluid circuit allows continuous power transmission as long as the prime mover drives the pump, with actuator output force directly proportional to system pressure and output velocity proportional to pump flow rate delivered to the actuator, which defines how a hydraulic system work. What Is the Working Principle of a Hydraulic System? The working principle of a hydraulic system rests on transmitting force through an incompressible fluid confined within a sealed circuit, where pressure applied at one point distributes equally throughout the fluid and acts on every pressure-exposed surface. The incompressibility of hydraulic oil (bulk modulus approximately 1,400 to 2,000 MPa) means fluid volume change under pressure is negligible, ensuring pump output flow translates directly into actuator displacement without energy absorption by the fluid itself. Pressure is generated at the pump by reducing the available volume of the fluid chamber, forcing fluid out against the resistance of the downstream load. The pressure level at any point in the circuit at steady state equals the load resistance divided by the actuator area: a 50 kN load on a 2,500 mm² piston requires 20 MPa of circuit pressure to maintain equilibrium. Pressure distributes evenly to every connected component, allowing efficient power transfer from a single pump to multiple actuators operating simultaneously at different pressures and flow rates through independent pressure-compensated control valves. Does a Hydraulic System Use Pressurized Fluid to Transmit Force? A hydraulic system uses pressurized fluid as its exclusive medium for transmitting force from the power source to the work output point. Fluid at pressure carries force in all directions through the circuit regardless of pipe routing, bends, or distance from the pump, allowing power transmission to locations inaccessible to mechanical shafts, gears, or linkages. A hydraulic excavator transmits engine power from the machine body through flexible high-pressure hoses to boom, arm, and bucket cylinders at the end of the arm structure, a configuration that mechanical transmission cannot replicate without complex and heavy linkage systems. The force carried by pressurized fluid is calculated as the product of pressure and the area over which it acts: F = P × A. At a working pressure of 30 MPa, a cylinder with a 100 mm bore (area 7,854 mm²) delivers 235 kN of pushing force, enabling mechanical work that far exceeds what pneumatic cylinders of equivalent size produce at typical operating pressures. What Are the Main Components of a Hydraulic System? The main components of a hydraulic system are listed below. Hydraulic Pump : The hydraulic pump converts mechanical energy from a prime mover into fluid flow and pressure. Gear pumps, vane pumps, and piston pumps are the primary types, operating at displacement volumes from 1 cm³ per revolution to over 500 cm³ per revolution at system pressures from 7 MPa to 70 MPa. The pump does not create pressure directly; pressure arises from the resistance of the load against which the pump delivers flow. Hydraulic Reservoir : The reservoir stores the system's fluid supply, holding 2 to 5 times the pump's per-minute flow rate to allow adequate fluid cooling, air release, and contaminant settling. Reservoir volumes in mobile equipment range from 50 liters to 500 liters; industrial press systems hold from 500 liters to several thousand liters. Hydraulic Actuators : Actuators convert fluid pressure energy into mechanical output. Linear actuators (hydraulic cylinders) produce pushing and pulling forces from 1 kN to over 100,000 kN; rotary actuators (hydraulic motors) produce torque from less than 1 N·m to over 100,000 N·m at speeds from 1 rpm to 10,000 rpm. Control Valves : Directional control valves route flow to selected actuator ports; pressure control valves (relief, reducing, sequence, counterbalance) manage pressure levels throughout the circuit; flow control valves regulate actuator speed. Valve operating pressures match system maximums, from 7 to 70 MPa. Hydraulic Fluid : Hydraulic fluid fills the circuit and acts as the force-transmission medium, lubricant, and heat-transfer agent. Mineral oils (ISO VG 32 to VG 100), fire-resistant fluids, and biodegradable vegetable-based fluids are selected based on operating temperature and seal compatibility. Filters and Strainers : Filters remove particulate contamination from the fluid to maintain cleanliness levels of ISO 4406 Class 16/14/11 or better, protecting pump and valve clearances (5 to 25 µm) from abrasive wear. Return line filters of 10 µm absolute rating are standard in industrial systems. Heat Exchanger (Oil Cooler) : The heat exchanger rejects heat generated by pump inefficiency and throttling losses, maintaining fluid temperature below 60°C to 70°C to prevent viscosity breakdown, seal degradation, and accelerated oxidation. Accumulators : Hydraulic accumulators store pressurized fluid (piston, bladder, or diaphragm types at pre-charge pressures of 50 to 80% of system pressure) to supply peak flow demands, dampen pressure spikes, and maintain pressure during pump shutdown. How Do Pumps and Actuators Function in a Hydraulic System? Pumps and actuators function in a hydraulic system through the conversion of mechanical energy into fluid pressure and the transformation of that pressure into controlled mechanical motion. Pumps and actuators in a hydraulic system draw hydraulic oil from the reservoir and deliver it under pressure into the system circuit, providing the energy input that drives all downstream motion. A fixed-displacement gear pump at 1,500 rpm with a 25 cm³/rev displacement delivers 37.5 liters per minute regardless of system pressure; a variable-displacement axial piston pump adjusts swashplate angle to modulate flow from near-zero to maximum based on actuator demand, reducing energy consumption by 30 to 50% compared to fixed-displacement alternatives in variable-load applications. Actuators receive pressurized flow from the pump and convert the fluid's pressure energy into mechanical output. A double-acting hydraulic cylinder uses differential piston areas on its extend and retract sides: at 20 MPa with a 100 mm bore and 70 mm rod, extension generates 157 kN of push force. Hydraulic motors convert flow and pressure into continuous rotary torque output, with torque proportional to displacement and pressure: a 100 cm³/rev motor at 20 MPa delivers approximately 318 N·m of output torque. The coordinated operation of the pump and actuator determines system force, speed, and total power consumption in every hydraulic circuit. How Do Actuators Function in a Hydraulic System? Actuators function in a hydraulic system by converting fluid pressure into mechanical motion that performs physical work. A hydraulic actuator receives pressurized fluid from the pump, which creates force when the fluid acts on internal components such as pistons or vanes. Pressure acting on a confined area generates force, which drives movement in a controlled direction. Is a Hydraulic Pump Responsible for Creating Fluid Flow? A hydraulic pump is responsible for creating fluid flow within a hydraulic system. No fluid circulates, no pressure builds at the actuator, and no mechanical work is performed without pump operation. The pump draws fluid from the reservoir through an inlet strainer and delivers it into the pressure line at a flow rate determined by its displacement and rotational speed: a gear pump with an 18 cm³/rev displacement running at 1,450 rpm delivers approximately 26 liters per minute. Flow, not pressure, is the pump's primary output. Pressure develops downstream of the pump only because the load or a control valve resists the flow. A pump running against a closed valve builds pressure to the relief valve setting (20 MPa) but delivers zero net flow to an actuator; a pump running against no resistance delivers maximum flow at near-zero pressure. Flow enables actuator velocity; pressure enables actuator force output in every hydraulic circuit. What Is the Role of Hydraulic Fluid in a Hydraulic System? The role of hydraulic fluid in a hydraulic system is to transmit power as the pressurized medium through which force transfers from pump to actuator, lubricating all moving components to reduce friction and wear, and removing heat generated by system inefficiencies to maintain operating temperature within acceptable limits. At working pressures of 20 to 70 MPa, hydraulic fluid carries energy from the pump to actuators with transmission efficiencies of 90 to 97% in well-maintained systems. Piston-to-bore clearances (3 to 10 µm) at pump gear teeth, spool valve clearances (5 to 20 µm), and bearing surfaces, the fluid maintains hydrodynamic or boundary lubrication films that prevent metal-to-metal contact. Circulating through the reservoir and oil cooler, the fluid rejects 20 to 40% of input power lost through throttling, friction, and leakage. Fluid degradation through oxidation, contamination, or viscosity loss reduces performance across all three functions simultaneously, making fluid condition monitoring a critical aspect of hydraulic fluid system maintenance. Xometry's hydraulic component specifications include fluid compatibility guidance for all seals, coatings, and bearing materials used in manufactured assemblies. Why Is Fluid Selection Important for Hydraulic System Performance? Fluid selection is important for hydraulic system performance because it determines viscosity, lubricity, thermal stability, and seal compatibility across the operating temperature range of the system, all of which directly govern efficiency, wear rate, and service intervals. Viscosity is the most critical property: hydraulic system components are designed for a specific viscosity range (ISO VG 32 to VG 68, or 32 to 68 centistokes at 40°C). A fluid too viscous for the operating temperature increases pressure drop through lines and valves, raising power losses and heat generation; a fluid too thin fails to maintain adequate lubricant film thickness at pump and motor running clearances, accelerating wear and reducing component life. Fluid with a high viscosity index (VI above 150 for premium mineral oils, above 200 for VI-improved synthetics) maintains near-constant viscosity across a temperature range from -20°C to 80°C, supporting consistent system performance through seasonal temperature changes in mobile equipment. Incorrect fluid selection (using a standard mineral oil in a system designed for phosphate-ester fire-resistant fluid) causes seal swelling, varnish deposits, and accelerated oxidation, reducing component life by 40 to 70% relative to a correctly specified fluid. Does Hydraulic Fluid Affect Efficiency and Component Life? Hydraulic fluid affects system efficiency and component service life. Volumetric efficiency (the ratio of actual to theoretical pump output) drops by 2 to 5 percentage points when fluid viscosity falls below the minimum recommended value for the pump, because thin fluid leaks past internal clearances, reducing flow delivered to actuators. Mechanical efficiency loss from inadequate lubrication film at bearing and spool surfaces adds a further 1 to 3% penalty to total system efficiency. Component life reductions from poor fluid condition are well-documented: gear and piston pumps operating at ISO cleanliness code above Class 20/18/15 experience bearing and gear wear rates 3 to 5 times higher than pumps supplied with Class 16/14/11 fluid. Fluid oxidation products (varnish and sludge) deposit on valve spools and accumulator bladders, increasing stiction forces and reducing valve response. Maintaining fluid cleanliness, viscosity, and additive condition within specification extends pump and motor service life from 5,000 to 10,000 hours to over 20,000 hours in well-maintained industrial systems. How Is Fluid Mechanics Applied in Hydraulic Systems? Fluid Mechanics is applied in hydraulic systems by governing how pressurized liquids transmit force, flow through components, and convert energy into mechanical work. Fluid Mechanics principles govern every aspect of hydraulic system behavior, from pressure generation at the pump through flow distribution in the circuit to energy recovery and loss at control components. The three foundational principles applied in hydraulic system design and analysis are Pascal's Law (pressure transmission), Bernoulli's equation (energy conservation in flowing fluid), and the continuity equation (conservation of mass, relating flow velocity to pipe cross-sectional area). Bernoulli's equation quantifies the relationship between pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy in a flowing fluid, predicting pressure drop across orifices, valve ports, and pipe bends. At a flow control orifice in a hydraulic circuit, fluid velocity increases as the cross-section decreases, converting pressure energy to kinetic energy: at 20 liters per minute through a 2 mm orifice, fluid mechanics velocity reaches approximately 10.6 m/s, generating a pressure drop that controls actuator speed. The continuity equation requires that flow velocity in a smaller pipe section is higher than in a larger section by the ratio of their areas, which hydraulic circuit designers use to size distribution lines for acceptable velocity limits (2 to 4 m/s in pressure lines, 1 to 2 m/s in return lines) to minimize friction losses and noise. What Fluid Mechanics Principles Control Hydraulic Pressure and Flow? The fluid mechanics principles that control hydraulic pressure and flow are listed below. Pascal's Law : Pascal's Law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid at rest transmits equally in all directions throughout the fluid. In hydraulic systems, the law governs force multiplication: the ratio of output force to input force equals the ratio of actuator area to pump piston area, enabling a pump delivering 5 kN of input force to generate 250 kN at a cylinder with 50 times the piston area at the same pressure. Bernoulli's Principle : Bernoulli's principle states that in a flowing fluid, an increase in velocity results in a decrease in pressure when elevation is constant. In hydraulic systems, the principle predicts pressure drops across valve orifices and port transitions, where high-velocity fluid at restricted passages loses static pressure, creating pressure differentials that circuit designers account for in valve sizing and line dimensioning. Continuity Equation : The continuity equation (A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ for incompressible flow) states that the product of cross-sectional area and fluid velocity is constant throughout a pipe of varying diameter. Halving the pipe diameter quadruples flow velocity, raising friction losses by approximately 16 times, making line sizing one of the most leverage-sensitive design decisions in hydraulic circuit layout. Hagen-Poiseuille Law : The Hagen-Poiseuille law governs laminar flow pressure drop in circular pipes: ΔP = (128 × µ × L × Q) / (π × D⁴), where µ is dynamic viscosity, L is pipe length, Q is volumetric flow rate, and D is pipe diameter. The fourth-power dependence on diameter means doubling the pipe bore reduces the friction pressure drop by a factor of 16. Reynolds Number : Reynolds number (Re = ρVD/µ) predicts flow regime: Re below 2,300 indicates laminar flow (smooth, low-loss), Re above 4,000 indicates turbulent flow (higher friction and noise). Hydraulic pressure lines target laminar or transitional flow (Re from 1,000 to 3,000) by sizing pipe diameter for fluid velocities of 2 to 4 m/s at maximum flow rate. Is Pascal's Law a Core Principle in Hydraulic System Design? Pascal's Law is the foundational core principle of hydraulic system design, providing the theoretical basis for force multiplication, pressure transmission, and load-holding behavior. Every hydraulic system function, from clamping force generation in a press to brake force distribution in a vehicle, depends directly on Pascal's Law operating in a closed fluid circuit. In practical design, Pascal's Law enables engineers to calculate actuator force output from known system pressure and piston area (F = P × A), size the pump output pressure for the required load capacity, and verify that every component in the circuit (hose, fitting, valve, cylinder body) is rated to withstand the maximum system pressure set by the relief valve. The law explains load-holding behavior: a cylinder supporting a static load holds its position without continuous pump energy input because the sealed fluid column transmits the load pressure back to the closed valve, maintaining equilibrium at zero flow. How Does Shear Stress Affect Hydraulic System Operation? Shear stress affects hydraulic system operation by determining the internal resistance of the fluid to flow, directly affecting the pressure energy consumed in moving fluid through pipes, valves, and component clearances. Shear stress in a fluid is defined as the tangential force per unit area acting from adjacent fluid layers moving at different velocities, calculated as τ = µ × (dv/dy), where µ is dynamic viscosity and dv/dy is the velocity gradient across the fluid layer (shear rate). In hydraulic lines and valve passages, shear stress generates a pressure drop that reduces the pressure available at the actuator relative to pump outlet pressure. At the running clearances of a hydraulic pump (piston-to-bore gap of 3 to 10 µm), shear stress in the fluid film produces viscous drag torque that reduces mechanical efficiency by 2 to 8%, depending on fluid viscosity and rotational speed. Higher shear stress increases internal energy loss, converting hydraulic power to heat: in a system operating at 30 MPa and 60 liters per minute, a 5% increase in friction losses from elevated shear stress dissipates an additional 1.5 kW as heat, raising oil temperature and accelerating fluid degradation. Why Is Shear Stress Important in Hydraulic Fluid Flow? Shear stress is important in hydraulic fluid flow, as it determines how fluid layers interact during relative motion, controlling flow resistance throughout every passage, clearance, and orifice in the circuit. In a pipe of radius R carrying laminar flow, the shear stress distribution is parabolic: maximum shear stress τ_w at the wall equals (4 × µ × Q) / (π × R³), and zero at the pipe centerline. The wall shear stress determines the pressure drop per unit length of pipe, which circuit designers minimize by selecting appropriate pipe diameters and fluid viscosity for the operating temperature range. The shear stress in the oil film from moving and stationary surfaces generates the lubricant layer that prevents metal-to-metal contact: if shear stress exceeds the fluid's shear strength at the operating viscosity and speed at pump and motor running clearances, the film collapses, allowing boundary lubrication or dry contact. Fluid additives (anti-wear zinc dithiophosphate at 0.05 to 0.15% concentration) form a sacrificial boundary film that maintains a minimum shear resistance layer, protecting metal surfaces when hydrodynamic film thickness drops below 0.5 µm during startup or at low-speed high-load operation. Can High Shear Stress Reduce Hydraulic System Efficiency? High shear stress reduces hydraulic system efficiency by increasing the pressure energy required to move fluid through the circuit, converting hydraulic power to heat rather than useful actuator output. Shear stress increases with fluid viscosity and flow velocity: operating a hydraulic system at oil temperatures below the recommended minimum (causing viscosity above VG 100 at operating conditions) raises shear stress in all passages, increasing circuit pressure losses by 10 to 25% relative to operation at the correct viscosity range. The direct efficiency penalty from elevated shear stress manifests as reduced overall system efficiency (η = P_out / P_in). In an excavator hydraulic system consuming 100 kW of engine input power, a 10% increase in circuit friction losses from high shear stress wastes an additional 10 kW as heat, reducing available digging force and raising oil temperature toward the degradation threshold of 80°C to 90°C. Correcting fluid viscosity to the recommended ISO VG grade for the ambient temperature range recovers the efficiency loss and returns oil temperature to the normal operating range of 40°C to 60°C. How Do Hydraulic Systems Influence Burst Strength Testing? Hydraulic Systems influence burst strength testing by applying controlled internal fluid pressure to a specimen until structural failure occurs. Hydraulic systems apply controlled, measurable pressure to test specimens in burst strength testing, providing the most accurate and repeatable method for determining the maximum pressure a material, hose, pipe, or vessel withstands before structural failure. The hydraulic test circuit generates pressure at precise increments using a manually or automatically controlled pump, filling the specimen with hydraulic fluid (or water in hydrostatic testing) and raising internal pressure at a controlled rate until the specimen ruptures or deforms to the failure criterion. The hydraulic method replicates real service conditions for pressure-containing components because the same incompressible fluid pressure that loads the component in service loads it during testing. Burst test systems for hose assemblies (per SAE J517 and EN ISO 6945) apply pressure at a rate of 2 MPa per second to 35 MPa per second until rupture, with the burst pressure recorded to ±0.1 MPa accuracy. Hydraulic burst strength test rigs for pipes and fittings (ASTM D1599 for plastic pipe, ASTM A999 for steel pipe) operate at pressures from 0.5 MPa to 700 MPa, depending on specimen material and wall thickness, simulating decades of pressure cycling within hours through accelerated fatigue protocols. What Is the Connection Between Hydraulic Pressure and Burst Strength? The connection between hydraulic pressure and burst strength lies in the direct relationship between internal fluid pressure and the maximum stress a material withstands before rupture. Burst strength is the maximum internal pressure a component sustains before catastrophic failure, and hydraulic pressure is the standard loading medium used to measure it because of its controllability, incompressibility, and ability to fill complex internal geometries uniformly. The burst pressure of a cylindrical pressure vessel or pipe is predicted by the Barlow formula: P_burst = (2 × S × t) / D, where S is the material's ultimate tensile strength, t is the wall thickness, and D is the outside diameter. Testing with hydraulic pressure verifies the calculated burst value and accounts for material variability, weld quality, and surface finish effects not captured by analytical prediction alone. The relationship from hydraulic operating pressure to burst strength defines the safety factor for pressure system design: hydraulic hose assemblies per SAE J517 require a minimum burst pressure of 4 times the maximum working pressure (safety factor 4:1), while hydraulic cylinders and manifold blocks carry burst pressure ratings of 2.5 to 4 times the nominal working pressure. Knowing the burst strength from hydraulic testing allows designers to set relief valve pressures, pressure transducer ranges, and proof test pressures for new component qualification. Is Hydraulic Pressure Used to Test Burst Strength in Pipes and Hoses? Hydraulic pressure is used to test the burst strength of pipes, hoses, fittings, and pressure vessels across all major industry standards. ASTM D1599 specifies hydraulic proof and burst testing for plastic pipe and fittings by pressurizing the specimen with water at a constant pressure rise rate until failure, recording the burst pressure and failure mode. SAE J517 and EN ISO 6945 require hydraulic burst testing of hose assemblies at 4 times the rated working pressure, with the hose filled with petroleum oil or water-glycol fluid at ambient temperature. Hydraulic pressure testing is preferred over pneumatic testing for burst applications because an incompressible fluid releases minimal stored energy at the moment of specimen failure, limiting the violence of the rupture event. A 300 mm diameter pipe section at 10 MPa stores approximately 0.15 joules of energy in compressed hydraulic fluid; the same specimen pressurized with compressed air stores over 1,000 joules, making pneumatic burst testing a serious safety hazard at high pressures. How Are Hydraulic Systems Used in Industrial Machines? Hydraulic systems that are used in Industrial Machines are listed below. Hydraulic Presses : Metal-forming and stamping presses use hydraulic cylinders to deliver compressive forces from 500 kN to over 100,000 kN for blanking, deep drawing, forging, and powder compaction. Hydraulic presses outperform mechanical presses in force controllability: pressure can be held constant at any position in the stroke, enabling isostatic pressing, embossing, and die-tryout operations not achievable with crank-driven mechanical presses. Injection Molding Machines : Hydraulic systems power the clamping unit, injection unit, and ejector mechanism of injection molding machines. The clamping cylinder generates forces from 500 kN to 55,000 kN to keep mold halves closed against injection pressure (70 to 200 MPa), while the injection cylinder drives the screw forward at controlled velocities to fill the mold cavity in 0.1 to 10 seconds. Excavators and Mobile Construction Equipment : Excavator hydraulic systems operate at pressures from 30 to 50 MPa, powering boom, arm, bucket, and swing circuits through load-sensing variable-displacement piston pumps with total flow rates of 200 to 800 liters per minute on large machines. The hydraulic system converts diesel engine power (100 to 500 kW) into digging, lifting, and swing torques with overall system efficiencies of 70 to 85%. Tensile and Compression Testing Machines : Servo-hydraulic universal testing machines apply precise tensile, compressive, or cyclic loads from 1 kN to 10,000 kN to material specimens, with load control accuracy of ±0.5% of indicated load per ASTM E4. The hydraulic actuator maintains constant load rates from 0.001 kN/s to 100 kN/s for quasi-static and high-rate material characterization testing. Hydraulic Turbines (Power Generation) : Hydraulic turbines in hydroelectric power stations convert water pressure energy to rotational shaft power using Francis, Pelton, or Kaplan runner designs, operating at heads from 2 m to over 1,800 m and generating power from 1 MW to over 800 MW per unit. The governing hydraulic system controls inlet guide vane position to regulate turbine output within ±0.1% of nominal frequency. Aircraft Flight Control Actuators : Aircraft primary and secondary flight control actuators operate at hydraulic system pressures of 20.7 MPa (3,000 psi) in legacy aircraft and 34.5 MPa (5,000 psi) in modern composite aircraft, powering aileron, elevator, rudder, and spoiler surfaces through electrohydraulic servo valves with frequency response above 10 Hz at full actuator stroke. How Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Use Hydraulic Power? Plastic injection molding machines use hydraulic power to drive the four primary machine functions: mold clamping, screw rotation and retraction, injection, and part ejection. The clamping unit uses a large-bore hydraulic cylinder (bore diameters from 200 mm to 800 mm) to close and lock the mold halves together with forces from 500 kN to 55,000 kN, maintaining closure against the injection pressure of 70 to 200 MPa that acts across the entire projected area of the cavity and runner system. The injection unit uses a hydraulic cylinder to drive the reciprocating screw forward at controlled injection velocity (20 to 150 mm/s), forcing molten plastic into the mold cavity in 0.1 to 10 seconds. A separate hydraulic motor rotates the screw during the plastication phase at 50 to 200 rpm, melting and metering the plastic charge for the next shot. Hydraulic pressure drives the ejector cylinder to push finished parts from the mold at forces of 10 to 500 kN after cooling, completing the cycle. The precision force and position control of the hydraulic circuits directly determines wall thickness uniformity, sink mark prevention, and part dimensional accuracy in plastic injection molding . How Do Tensile Testing Machines Use Hydraulic Power? Tensile testing machines use hydraulic power to apply controlled tensile, compressive, and cyclic forces to material specimens, measuring mechanical properties including tensile strength, yield strength, elongation, and fracture toughness. The hydraulic actuator (single or double-acting cylinder, bore diameter 50 to 400 mm) generates test loads from 1 kN to 10,000 kN at load control accuracies of ±0.5% of the indicated value, meeting ASTM E4 and ISO 7500-1 verification standards for universal testing machines. A servo-hydraulic control system regulates actuator displacement, load, or strain at rates from 0.001 mm/min in creep testing to 20,000 mm/min in high-rate tensile testing, with closed-loop feedback from a load cell and extensometer maintaining the commanded test parameter within ±0.1%. Hydraulic pressure in high-cycle fatigue testing machines cycles at frequencies from 0.1 Hz to 100 Hz, applying sinusoidal or block loading spectra to simulate service loading histories over 10⁶ to 10⁸ cycles. The hydraulic actuator's combination of high force capacity, precise control, and bidirectional loading capability makes it the preferred force-generation method for mechanical property characterization in materials tensile testing machines and laboratories. Do Injection Molding and Tensile Testing Machines Use Hydraulic Pressure? Injection molding and tensile testing machines use hydraulic pressure as their primary force generation method, relying on controlled fluid pressure to deliver the high forces and precise motion control their operations require. In injection molding, hydraulic pressure at 7 to 21 MPa in the machine's hydraulic circuit generates clamping forces of 500 to 55,000 kN and injection pressures of 70 to 200 MPa at the mold cavity, enabling the precise filling and solidification of complex plastic part geometries. In tensile testing, a servo-hydraulic actuator applies controlled loads from 1 kN to 10,000 kN at closed-loop accuracy of ±0.5% of indicated load, producing the force-displacement data needed to characterize material mechanical properties per ASTM and ISO standards. The hydraulic pressure circuit in injection molding and tensile testing machines delivers force levels, control precision, and sustained duty cycle performance that electric motor-driven alternatives of equivalent force rating require significantly larger and more expensive drive systems to match. What Safety Risks Are Common in Hydraulic Systems? The safety risks common in hydraulic systems are listed below. High-Pressure Fluid Injection : Hydraulic fluid escaping from a pinhole leak at pressures of 7 to 70 MPa penetrates skin and tissue with a jet velocity sufficient to cause serious injury or amputation without visible external wounding. Fluid injection injuries require immediate surgical debridement; delay of more than 6 hours significantly increases tissue loss. The risk is present at all pressurized fittings, hose connections, and cylinder rod seals. Hose and Fitting Failure : Hydraulic hoses fatigue from repeated pressure cycling, abrasion against surrounding structures, and UV degradation of the outer cover, leading to sudden burst or whip failure. A hose operating at 35 MPa that fails without containment releases a high-velocity fluid stream and a whipping hose end generating impact forces above 500 N. Inspection intervals of 12 months maximum and replacement at first signs of cover cracking or bulging are standard practice per ISO 4413. Hydraulic Oil Fire : Petroleum-based hydraulic oil with a flash point of 150°C to 185°C ignites upon contact with a hot surface (exhaust manifolds at 400°C to 600°C) or an open flame when atomized from a high-pressure leak. Fire-resistant hydraulic fluids (water-glycol, phosphate-ester, or polyol-ester types) are mandatory in steel mills, die casting, and underground mining per EN ISO 12922. Stored Energy Release : A hydraulic accumulator pre-charged to 70 to 80% of system pressure (up to 56 MPa) stores sufficient energy to cause lethal ejection of components if disassembled without first discharging the accumulator to zero pressure. Proper lock-out/tag-out procedures require pressure relief at the accumulator isolation valve before any maintenance activity. Cylinder Drift and Load Drop : Internal leakage across worn cylinder seals or directional valve spools allows a loaded cylinder to drift under gravity, dropping suspended loads or closing mold platens unexpectedly. Load-holding (counterbalance) valves mounted directly at the cylinder port and rated at 1.3 to 1.5 times the maximum load-induced pressure prevent drift in vertical and overhead actuator applications. Thermal Overload : Continuous operation at fluid temperatures above 80°C to 90°C degrades oil viscosity and additive packages, accelerating seal wear, pump cavitation from vapor formation, and oxidative varnish deposits on valve spools. An overheating hydraulic system in a continuous-duty industrial press loses 15 to 30% of pump volumetric efficiency within 500 operating hours without corrective action. sections.heading: What Is a Hydraulic System?
sections.text: What Is a Hydraulic System? A hydraulic system is a mechanical power transmission system that uses a pressurized, incompressible liquid to generate, control, and transfer force to perform useful work. The system relies on controlled fluid movement through interconnected components, producing linear force from cylinders or rotary torque from motors, with outputs ranging from a few kilonewtons in precision equipment to over 100,000 kN in large industrial presses. Hydraulic systems are widely used in industrial and mobile machinery because fluid power transmits large forces through small-diameter lines with precise controllability. An excavator boom generates digging forces exceeding 150 kN from a hydraulic cylinder with a 150 mm bore diameter at a working pressure of 35 MPa, a force-to-size ratio unachievable with comparable mechanical linkages. Industrial machinery, including injection molding machines, metal-forming presses, and material testing frames, depends on hydraulic systems for high force density (power output per unit volume), smooth motion control, and the ability to hold loads statically without continuous energy input. sections.heading: How Is a Hydraulic System Defined in Engineering?
sections.text: How Is a Hydraulic System Defined in Engineering? A hydraulic system is defined in engineering as a power transmission system that converts mechanical input energy into fluid pressure energy at a pump, transmits that pressure energy through a fluid circuit, and reconverts it to mechanical output energy at an actuator to perform work. The definition encompasses the full energy conversion chain: a prime mover (electric motor or combustion engine) drives a hydraulic pump, which pressurizes fluid and delivers it at controlled flow rates through distribution lines to cylinders, motors, or other actuators that execute the required mechanical motion. Hydraulic systems are essential in heavy equipment because they transmit power efficiently over distance through flexible hoses, allow force multiplication through differential piston areas, and provide inherently overload-protected operation through pressure relief valves set at the maximum allowable working pressure. Operating pressures in industrial hydraulic systems range from 7 MPa in light-duty mobile equipment to 70 MPa in high-force hydraulic presses and forming machines. sections.heading: How Does a Hydraulic System Work?
sections.text: How Does a Hydraulic System Work? A hydraulic system works by pressurizing incompressible fluid at a pump, directing it through control valves and distribution lines to actuators, where fluid pressure acts on piston or vane surfaces to generate mechanical force and motion. The pump draws fluid from a reservoir, raises its pressure from near-atmospheric to the system's working pressure (7 to 70 MPa), and delivers it at a controlled volumetric flow rate into the pressure circuit. Directional control valves route pressurized fluid to the correct actuator port, determining the direction of cylinder extension or motor rotation. Pressure control valves set the maximum operating pressure and manage load-holding behavior, while flow control valves regulate actuator speed by restricting fluid volume per unit time. Return fluid from the low-pressure side of the actuator flows back through the return line to the reservoir, where it is filtered, cooled, and recirculated. The closed-loop fluid circuit allows continuous power transmission as long as the prime mover drives the pump, with actuator output force directly proportional to system pressure and output velocity proportional to pump flow...

sections.heading: What Is the Working Principle of a Hydraulic System?
sections.text: What Is the Working Principle of a Hydraulic System? The working principle of a hydraulic system rests on transmitting force through an incompressible fluid confined within a sealed circuit, where pressure applied at one point distributes equally throughout the fluid and acts on every pressure-exposed surface. The incompressibility of hydraulic oil (bulk modulus approximately 1,400 to 2,000 MPa) means fluid volume change under pressure is negligible, ensuring pump output flow translates directly into actuator displacement without energy absorption by the fluid itself. Pressure is generated at the pump by reducing the available volume of the fluid chamber, forcing fluid out against the resistance of the downstream load. The pressure level at any point in the circuit at steady state equals the load resistance divided by the actuator area: a 50 kN load on a 2,500 mm² piston requires 20 MPa of circuit pressure to maintain equilibrium. Pressure distributes evenly to every connected component, allowing efficient power transfer from a single pump to multiple actuators operating simultaneously at different pressures and flow rates through independent pressure-compensated control valves. sections.heading: What Are the Main Components of a Hydraulic System?
sections.text: What Are the Main Components of a Hydraulic System? The main components of a hydraulic system are listed below. Hydraulic Pump : The hydraulic pump converts mechanical energy from a prime mover into fluid flow and pressure. Gear pumps, vane pumps, and piston pumps are the primary types, operating at displacement volumes from 1 cm³ per revolution to over 500 cm³ per revolution at system pressures from 7 MPa to 70 MPa. The pump does not create pressure directly; pressure arises from the resistance of the load against which the pump delivers flow. Hydraulic Reservoir : The reservoir stores the system's fluid supply, holding 2 to 5 times the pump's per-minute flow rate to allow adequate fluid cooling, air release, and contaminant settling. Reservoir volumes in mobile equipment range from 50 liters to 500 liters; industrial press systems hold from 500 liters to several thousand liters. Hydraulic Actuators : Actuators convert fluid pressure energy into mechanical output. Linear actuators (hydraulic cylinders) produce pushing and pulling forces from 1 kN to over 100,000 kN; rotary actuators (hydraulic motors) produce torque from less than 1 N·m to over 100,000 N·m at speeds from 1 rpm to...

sections.heading: How Do Pumps and Actuators Function in a Hydraulic System?
sections.text: How Do Pumps and Actuators Function in a Hydraulic System? Pumps and actuators function in a hydraulic system through the conversion of mechanical energy into fluid pressure and the transformation of that pressure into controlled mechanical motion. Pumps and actuators in a hydraulic system draw hydraulic oil from the reservoir and deliver it under pressure into the system circuit, providing the energy input that drives all downstream motion. A fixed-displacement gear pump at 1,500 rpm with a 25 cm³/rev displacement delivers 37.5 liters per minute regardless of system pressure; a variable-displacement axial piston pump adjusts swashplate angle to modulate flow from near-zero to maximum based on actuator demand, reducing energy consumption by 30 to 50% compared to fixed-displacement alternatives in variable-load applications. Actuators receive pressurized flow from the pump and convert the fluid's pressure energy into mechanical output. A double-acting hydraulic cylinder uses differential piston areas on its extend and retract sides: at 20 MPa with a 100 mm bore and 70 mm rod, extension generates 157 kN of push force. Hydraulic motors convert flow and pressure into continuous rotary...

sections.heading: What Is the Role of Hydraulic Fluid in a Hydraulic System?
sections.text: What Is the Role of Hydraulic Fluid in a Hydraulic System? The role of hydraulic fluid in a hydraulic system is to transmit power as the pressurized medium through which force transfers from pump to actuator, lubricating all moving components to reduce friction and wear, and removing heat generated by system inefficiencies to maintain operating temperature within acceptable limits. At working pressures of 20 to 70 MPa, hydraulic fluid carries energy from the pump to actuators with transmission efficiencies of 90 to 97% in well-maintained systems. Piston-to-bore clearances (3 to 10 µm) at pump gear teeth, spool valve clearances (5 to 20 µm), and bearing surfaces, the fluid maintains hydrodynamic or boundary lubrication films that prevent metal-to-metal contact. Circulating through the reservoir and oil cooler, the fluid rejects 20 to 40% of input power lost through throttling, friction, and leakage. Fluid degradation through oxidation, contamination, or viscosity loss reduces performance across all three functions simultaneously, making fluid condition monitoring a critical aspect of hydraulic fluid system maintenance. sections.heading: Why Is Fluid Selection Important for Hydraulic System Performance?
sections.text: Why Is Fluid Selection Important for Hydraulic System Performance? Fluid selection is important for hydraulic system performance because it determines viscosity, lubricity, thermal stability, and seal compatibility across the operating temperature range of the system, all of which directly govern efficiency, wear rate, and service intervals. Viscosity is the most critical property: hydraulic system components are designed for a specific viscosity range (ISO VG 32 to VG 68, or 32 to 68 centistokes at 40°C). A fluid too viscous for the operating temperature increases pressure drop through lines and valves, raising power losses and heat generation; a fluid too thin fails to maintain adequate lubricant film thickness at pump and motor running clearances, accelerating wear and reducing component life. Fluid with a high viscosity index (VI above 150 for premium mineral oils, above 200 for VI-improved synthetics) maintains near-constant viscosity across a temperature range from -20°C to 80°C, supporting consistent system performance through seasonal temperature changes in mobile equipment. Incorrect fluid selection (using a standard mineral oil in a system designed for phosphate-ester fi...

sections.heading: How Is Fluid Mechanics Applied in Hydraulic Systems?
sections.text: How Is Fluid Mechanics Applied in Hydraulic Systems? Fluid Mechanics is applied in hydraulic systems by governing how pressurized liquids transmit force, flow through components, and convert energy into mechanical work. Fluid Mechanics principles govern every aspect of hydraulic system behavior, from pressure generation at the pump through flow distribution in the circuit to energy recovery and loss at control components. The three foundational principles applied in hydraulic system design and analysis are Pascal's Law (pressure transmission), Bernoulli's equation (energy conservation in flowing fluid), and the continuity equation (conservation of mass, relating flow velocity to pipe cross-sectional area). Bernoulli's equation quantifies the relationship between pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy in a flowing fluid, predicting pressure drop across orifices, valve ports, and pipe bends. At a flow control orifice in a hydraulic circuit, fluid velocity increases as the cross-section decreases, converting pressure energy to kinetic energy: at 20 liters per minute through a 2 mm orifice, fluid mechanics velocity reaches approximately 10.6 m/s, generating a pressure d...

sections.heading: What Fluid Mechanics Principles Control Hydraulic Pressure and Flow?
sections.text: What Fluid Mechanics Principles Control Hydraulic Pressure and Flow? The fluid mechanics principles that control hydraulic pressure and flow are listed below. Pascal's Law : Pascal's Law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid at rest transmits equally in all directions throughout the fluid. In hydraulic systems, the law governs force multiplication: the ratio of output force to input force equals the ratio of actuator area to pump piston area, enabling a pump delivering 5 kN of input force to generate 250 kN at a cylinder with 50 times the piston area at the same pressure. Bernoulli's Principle : Bernoulli's principle states that in a flowing fluid, an increase in velocity results in a decrease in pressure when elevation is constant. In hydraulic systems, the principle predicts pressure drops across valve orifices and port transitions, where high-velocity fluid at restricted passages loses static pressure, creating pressure differentials that circuit designers account for in valve sizing and line dimensioning. sections.heading: How Does Shear Stress Affect Hydraulic System Operation?
sections.text: How Does Shear Stress Affect Hydraulic System Operation? Shear stress affects hydraulic system operation by determining the internal resistance of the fluid to flow, directly affecting the pressure energy consumed in moving fluid through pipes, valves, and component clearances. Shear stress in a fluid is defined as the tangential force per unit area acting from adjacent fluid layers moving at different velocities, calculated as τ = µ × (dv/dy), where µ is dynamic viscosity and dv/dy is the velocity gradient across the fluid layer (shear rate). In hydraulic lines and valve passages, shear stress generates a pressure drop that reduces the pressure available at the actuator relative to pump outlet pressure. At the running clearances of a hydraulic pump (piston-to-bore gap of 3 to 10 µm), shear stress in the fluid film produces viscous drag torque that reduces mechanical efficiency by 2 to 8%, depending on fluid viscosity and rotational speed. Higher shear stress increases internal energy loss, converting hydraulic power to heat: in a system operating at 30 MPa and 60 liters per minute, a 5% increase in friction losses from elevated shear stress dissipates an additional 1.5 kW as heat...

sections.heading: Why Is Shear Stress Important in Hydraulic Fluid Flow?
sections.text: Why Is Shear Stress Important in Hydraulic Fluid Flow? Shear stress is important in hydraulic fluid flow, as it determines how fluid layers interact during relative motion, controlling flow resistance throughout every passage, clearance, and orifice in the circuit. In a pipe of radius R carrying laminar flow, the shear stress distribution is parabolic: maximum shear stress τ_w at the wall equals (4 × µ × Q) / (π × R³), and zero at the pipe centerline. The wall shear stress determines the pressure drop per unit length of pipe, which circuit designers minimize by selecting appropriate pipe diameters and fluid viscosity for the operating temperature range. The shear stress in the oil film from moving and stationary surfaces generates the lubricant layer that prevents metal-to-metal contact: if shear stress exceeds the fluid's shear strength at the operating viscosity and speed at pump and motor running clearances, the film collapses, allowing boundary lubrication or dry contact. sections.heading: How Do Hydraulic Systems Influence Burst Strength Testing?
sections.text: How Do Hydraulic Systems Influence Burst Strength Testing? Hydraulic Systems influence burst strength testing by applying controlled internal fluid pressure to a specimen until structural failure occurs. Hydraulic systems apply controlled, measurable pressure to test specimens in burst strength testing, providing the most accurate and repeatable method for determining the maximum pressure a material, hose, pipe, or vessel withstands before structural failure. The hydraulic test circuit generates pressure at precise increments using a manually or automatically controlled pump, filling the specimen with hydraulic fluid (or water in hydrostatic testing) and raising internal pressure at a controlled rate until the specimen ruptures or deforms to the failure criterion. The hydraulic method replicates real service conditions for pressure-containing components because the same incompressible fluid pressure that loads the component in service loads it during testing. Burst test systems for hose assemblies (per SAE J517 and EN ISO 6945) apply pressure at a rate of 2 MPa per second to 35 MPa per second until rupture, with the burst pressure recorded to ±0.1 MPa accuracy. sections.heading: What Is the Connection Between Hydraulic Pressure and Burst Strength?
sections.text: What Is the Connection Between Hydraulic Pressure and Burst Strength? The connection between hydraulic pressure and burst strength lies in the direct relationship between internal fluid pressure and the maximum stress a material withstands before rupture. Burst strength is the maximum internal pressure a component sustains before catastrophic failure, and hydraulic pressure is the standard loading medium used to measure it because of its controllability, incompressibility, and ability to fill complex internal geometries uniformly. The burst pressure of a cylindrical pressure vessel or pipe is predicted by the Barlow formula: P_burst = (2 × S × t) / D, where S is the material's ultimate tensile strength, t is the wall thickness, and D is the outside diameter. Testing with hydraulic pressure verifies the calculated burst value and accounts for material variability, weld quality, and surface finish effects not captured by analytical prediction alone. sections.heading: How Are Hydraulic Systems Used in Industrial Machines?
sections.text: How Are Hydraulic Systems Used in Industrial Machines? Hydraulic systems that are used in Industrial Machines are listed below. Hydraulic Presses : Metal-forming and stamping presses use hydraulic cylinders to deliver compressive forces from 500 kN to over 100,000 kN for blanking, deep drawing, forging, and powder compaction. Hydraulic presses outperform mechanical presses in force controllability: pressure can be held constant at any position in the stroke, enabling isostatic pressing, embossing, and die-tryout operations not achievable with crank-driven mechanical presses. Injection Molding Machines : Hydraulic systems power the clamping unit, injection unit, and ejector mechanism of injection molding machines. The clamping cylinder generates forces from 500 kN to 55,000 kN to keep mold halves closed against injection pressure (70 to 200 MPa), while the injection cylinder drives the screw forward at controlled velocities to fill the mold cavity in 0.1 to 10 seconds. Excavators and Mobile Construction Equipment : Excavator hydraulic systems operate at pressures from 30 to 50 MPa, powering boom, arm, bucket, and swing circuits through load-sensing variable-displacement piston pump...

sections.heading: How Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Use Hydraulic Power?
sections.text: How Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Use Hydraulic Power? Plastic injection molding machines use hydraulic power to drive the four primary machine functions: mold clamping, screw rotation and retraction, injection, and part ejection. The clamping unit uses a large-bore hydraulic cylinder (bore diameters from 200 mm to 800 mm) to close and lock the mold halves together with forces from 500 kN to 55,000 kN, maintaining closure against the injection pressure of 70 to 200 MPa that acts across the entire projected area of the cavity and runner system. The injection unit uses a hydraulic cylinder to drive the reciprocating screw forward at controlled injection velocity (20 to 150 mm/s), forcing molten plastic into the mold cavity in 0.1 to 10 seconds. A separate hydraulic motor rotates the screw during the plastication phase at 50 to 200 rpm, melting and metering the plastic charge for the next shot. Hydraulic pressure drives the ejector cylinder to push finished parts from the mold at forces of 10 to 500 kN after cooling, completing the cycle. sections.heading: How Do Tensile Testing Machines Use Hydraulic Power?
sections.text: How Do Tensile Testing Machines Use Hydraulic Power? Tensile testing machines use hydraulic power to apply controlled tensile, compressive, and cyclic forces to material specimens, measuring mechanical properties including tensile strength, yield strength, elongation, and fracture toughness. The hydraulic actuator (single or double-acting cylinder, bore diameter 50 to 400 mm) generates test loads from 1 kN to 10,000 kN at load control accuracies of ±0.5% of the indicated value, meeting ASTM E4 and ISO 7500-1 verification standards for universal testing machines. A servo-hydraulic control system regulates actuator displacement, load, or strain at rates from 0.001 mm/min in creep testing to 20,000 mm/min in high-rate tensile testing, with closed-loop feedback from a load cell and extensometer maintaining the commanded test parameter within ±0.1%. Hydraulic pressure in high-cycle fatigue testing machines cycles at frequencies from 0.1 Hz to 100 Hz, applying sinusoidal or block loading spectra to simulate service loading histories over 10⁶ to 10⁸ cycles. sections.heading: What Safety Risks Are Common in Hydraulic Systems?
sections.text: What Safety Risks Are Common in Hydraulic Systems? The safety risks common in hydraulic systems are listed below. High-Pressure Fluid Injection : Hydraulic fluid escaping from a pinhole leak at pressures of 7 to 70 MPa penetrates skin and tissue with a jet velocity sufficient to cause serious injury or amputation without visible external wounding. Fluid injection injuries require immediate surgical debridement; delay of more than 6 hours significantly increases tissue loss. The risk is present at all pressurized fittings, hose connections, and cylinder rod seals. Hose and Fitting Failure : Hydraulic hoses fatigue from repeated pressure cycling, abrasion against surrounding structures, and UV degradation of the outer cover, leading to sudden burst or whip failure.
